hero.eyebrow: AI literacy · No coding, no AI account needed
hero.title: Prompt Engineering: ask better, check better
hero.subtitle: Write structured prompts in a document editor, score prompt versions and estimate costs in a working spreadsheet, and learn when to trust and when to verify. Every task is checked and explained.
hero.outcomeLine: After this course you can write clear prompts, test them, use AI responsibly and keep a reusable prompt library.

tools.title: Sort and decide
tools.text: Capabilities, prompt quality, techniques and privacy.

assessment: Finish the required labs in each module: they are checked automatically and explained when something is missing.
Pass each module quiz (70% or more). You can retry as often as you like.
Complete the prompt library and the final assessment.

faq.q: Does the course connect to an AI service?
faq.a: No. The labs check the structure and content of what you write, not an AI's reply. You can try your prompts in any assistant you use.

faq.q: Is it specific to one AI product?
faq.a: No. The principles apply to most modern assistants, and the course avoids relying on any one product's menus.

faq.q: Will the techniques go out of date?
faq.a: Tools change quickly. The course focuses on durable habits: clear instructions, supplying context, checking outputs and protecting privacy.

activities.title: Write a well-structured prompt
activities.objective: Write a prompt with a role, a task, context, constraints and an output format.
activities.scenario: You want an AI assistant to help plan a study timetable for the two weeks before exams. Write the prompt you would give it.
steps: Write short labelled lines starting with Role:, Task:, Context:, Constraints: and Format:.
In Context include your subjects and the exam dates (invent them).
In Constraints include limits such as maximum hours per day.
In Format say how you want the result (for example a table by day).
Keep it between 70 and 200 words.

activities.title: Score three versions of a prompt
activities.objective: Compare prompt versions with a simple scoring rubric and pick the best.
activities.scenario: You tried three versions of a prompt on five test inputs and scored each answer from 1 to 5. Compare the versions.
steps: In G2 find each version's average score with AVERAGE.
In H2 find its lowest score with MIN.
In I2 give a weighted result: 70% average plus 30% lowest score.
Fill the formulas down for all three versions.
In B8 name the best version by the highest weighted result using IF.

checks.label: G2 is V1's average
checks.hint: =AVERAGE(B2:F2)
checks.explain: The mean of the five scores.

checks.label: H3 is V2's lowest score
checks.hint: =MIN(B3:F3)

checks.label: I2 is the weighted result
checks.explain: Weight the average and the worst case.

checks.label: I4 is V3's weighted result
checks.hint: Fill down.

checks.label: B8 names the best version

activities.title: Estimate usage and cost
activities.objective: Estimate tokens and cost for a batch of AI requests so you can plan a budget.
activities.scenario: A small team will send 2,000 requests a month. Each prompt has about 300 words and each answer about 200 words. Roughly 1 word is 1.3 tokens. Use an illustrative price of 2 rupees per 1,000 tokens (check real prices before you plan).
steps: In B7 work out tokens per request: (prompt words + answer words) times the tokens per word in B4.
In B8 work out the tokens per month: tokens per request times requests per month (B5).
In B9 work out the monthly cost: tokens per month divided by 1000, times the price in B6.
In B10 work out the cost per request.

checks.label: B7 is tokens per request
B8 is tokens per month
checks.explain: Per request times the number of requests.

checks.label: B9 is the monthly cost
checks.explain: Thousands of tokens times the price.

checks.label: B10 is cost per request

activities.title: Final project: build a prompt library
activities.objective: Create three reusable, well-structured prompts with notes on how to check the output.
activities.scenario: Create a small prompt library for a student: one for summarising notes, one for making practice questions and one for improving writing.
steps: Add a Heading 1 'My prompt library'.
Add three Heading 2 sections, one per prompt, each with a clear name.
Under each, write a Prompt: line using placeholders in square brackets, such as [paste text here].
Under each, write a How I check it: line saying how you will verify the output.
Keep it between 150 and 340 words.
